facts.text: Basic relative error is the absolute difference between simulation and experiment divided by the experimental value.
facts.quote: The basic relative error is the absolute difference between simulation and experiment divided by the experimental value.

facts.text: FAA AC 20-146A uses 10% agreement criteria for several aircraft-seat quantities, including critical floor reaction loads, structural deformation, restraint loads and several injury outputs.
facts.quote: FAA AC 20-146A uses 10% agreement criteria for several aircraft-seat quantities, including critical floor reaction loads, structural deformation, restraint loads and several injury outputs

facts.text: FAA AC 20-146A allows other model-specific agreement criteria to be agreed with the certification authority.
facts.quote: while allowing other model-specific criteria to be agreed with the certification authority.

facts.text: The aircraft-seat agreement criteria in FAA AC 20-146A are application-specific and should not be copied as a generic 10% tolerance for off-road braking.
facts.quote: Those numbers belong to that application and should not be copied as a generic 10% tolerance for off-road braking.

facts.text: In the FAA worked example, a measured load peak of 1,315 lb and a simulated peak of 1,360 lb yield a relative peak error of 3.42%, calculated as (1360 minus 1315) divided by 1315.
facts.quote: a measured load peak of 1,315 lb and a simulated peak of 1,360 lb give (1360 minus 1315) divided by 1315, that is 3.42% peak error.

facts.text: The FAA worked example comparing a measured load peak of 1,315 lb with a simulated peak of 1,360 lb has a Sprague-Geers time-history error of 7.2%.
facts.quote: The same comparison has a Sprague-Geers time-history error of 7.2%.

facts.text: The FAA worked example's 3.42% peak error and 7.2% Sprague-Geers time-history error are both within the example's 10% guideline.
facts.quote: Both are within the FAA example's 10% guideline.
